human_tolerance.notes: Generalists that adapt to a wide variety of habitats and readily forage in farmyards, eating hay, grass and white clover as well as wild browse; a major wildlife conflict species in settled landscapes, and habituated animals can lose their fear of people.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: Females enter estrus, the rut, in the autumn, normally in late October or early November, triggered mainly by the declining photoperiod. Bucks spar to establish a dominance hierarchy and then court; they rarely eat or rest during the rut, and the rut is shorter in duration at higher latitude.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Females give birth to one to three spotted young, the fawns, in mid-to-late spring, generally May or June. For the first four weeks the fawns are hidden in vegetation and nursed four to five times a day, then follow their mothers on foraging trips; usually weaned after 8-10 weeks.

vocalizations.description: Breathing very heavily, also called blowing, in the presence of potential predators. The sound alerts other deer in the area, and the flash of the white tail as the deer runs warns them too.

A guttural grunt that attracts the attention of other deer in the area. Fawns start with a high-pitched squeal or bleat to call out to their mothers; the note deepens as the fawn grows until it becomes the mature deer's grunt. Does make maternal grunts when searching for bedded fawns, and bucks grunt at a lower pitch.
Both does and bucks snort, a sound that often signals an imminent threat.

taxonomy.note: GBIF backbone gives family Cervidae, order Artiodactyla and authority (Zimmermann, 1780); ITIS scientific-name search returns TSN 180699 with the same authority.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 2440965 from species/match; ITIS TSN 180699 from the ITIS scientific-name search; NCBI taxon id 9874 and IUCN category least concern (Q211005) from Wikidata P685 and P141. No eBird code applies to a mammal.

range.note: Native range from the species' North American and Neotropical distribution (the article treats Florida Key deer O. v. clavium and the Columbian white-tailed deer O. v. leucurus as members of this species, so the Central American and northern South American countries are included); introduced range from the explicit list, 'introduced (primarily for sport hunting) to New Zealand, Nova Scotia ..., Prince Edward Island ..., New Brunswick ..., the Greater Antilles of the Caribbean (Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola, and Puerto Rico), and some countries in Europe (mainly the Czech Republic, Finland, France, Germany, Romania and Serbia)'. Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick are omitted here because the article describes them as native in part or subsequently eradicated.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Walk, Trot and Gallop are all described: the species forages by browsing, moves between beds, and on alarm 'blows' and flees, with canids pursuing deer in an extended chase and predators going for the limbs and flanks.

traits.nest_type.note: None: the species builds no nest and the female gives birth standing, the fawns being hidden in vegetation rather than in a den or nest.

traits.perching.note: Not a perching animal; it browses, beds on the ground and uses thicket cover.

traits.senses.note: From the Description section: 'The white-tailed deer's horizontally slit pupil allows for good night vision and color vision during the day. Whitetails process visual images at a much more rapid rate than humans and are better at detecting motion in low-light conditions.' olfaction High from the Communication section, which lists scent marking as one of the species' main channels alongside sound and body language.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (65.7 kg is at or above the 50 kg Large threshold).

traits.mass_kg.note: Mean of EltonTraits MamFuncDat BodyMass-Value 55508.56 g and PanTHERIA AdultBodyMass_g 75901.25 g, giving 65.7 kg. The two sources bracket Wikipedia's North American figures (does 40-90 kg, bucks 68-136 kg), and the 183-232 kg field-dressed record buck is an extreme outlier not used.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: North American does usually 40-90 kg and bucks usually 68-136 kg; the range spans the lightest typical adult to the heaviest typical buck. The much larger record animals and the smaller tropical and Florida Keys populations are noted in the note on range rather than folded into this band.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of 95 to 220 cm, which the source states includes a tail of 10 to 37 cm. The midpoint is consistent with PanTHERIA's AdultHeadBodyLen of 1513.69 mm plus a short tail.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Judgement, and an honest gap: the Wikipedia article gives no lifespan figure, and no openly licensed source consulted states a mean or typical lifespan for this species. 6.0 years is an authored order-of-magnitude figure for a large ungulate whose dominant mortality source is predation, so most individuals do not reach old age. Treat it as a placeholder, not a measurement.

traits.home_range_ha.note: Judgement, and an honest gap: PanTHERIA gives no home-range value for this species and the Wikipedia article does not state one, though it does give a density of about 8 deer per square kilometre. 100 ha is an authored order-of-magnitude figure for the seasonal range of a large deer, not a sourced value.

traits.diet.note: EltonTraits Diet-PlantO 90 mapped to browse and Diet-Seed 10 mapped to mast. Wikipedia's Diet section agrees with that reading: 'Their diet consists mostly of woody shoots, stems, and leaves of woody plants as well as grasses, cultivated crops, nuts, berries, and wil[turkey oak acorns].' Grasses, cultivated crops and berries sit inside the sourced 90 rather than being split out, because the dataset does not separate them. The same section records that deer 'have been known to opportunistically feed on nesting songbirds, field mice, and birds trapped in mist nets, if the need arises'; that trace share is omitted from the fractions and noted here instead.

traits.social.note: Group from the source's account of does keeping fawns hidden and then accompanying them, of does making maternal grunts to search for bedded fawns, and of a blowing or snorting deer alerting 'other deer in the area'. 'Males leave their mothers after a year and females leave after two' and bucks spar for dominance, so the structure is loose groups rather than pairs or families; the upper bound of 8 is an authored figure, since the source does not count group size.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'crepuscular, meaning they are most active at dawn and dusk, sporadically resting throughout the day and night'.

traits.defense.note: 'White-tailed deer typically respond to the presence of potential predators by breathing very heavily (also called blowing) and fleeing', with tail-flagging warning other deer.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: a hunted and heavily human-associated species that is generally alert to people, but which also feeds in farmyards and readily habituates where it is not pressured.

habitat.use.note: EltonTraits ForStrat-Value 'G' gives the primary stratum as ground. The arboreal share of 0.1 is authored judgement for browsing shrub and canopy foliage, which the source describes directly ('woody shoots, stems, and leaves of woody plants').

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Authored: the species beds in cover, and the source repeatedly refers to does searching for bedded fawns and to thicket use; shrub_thicket is the schema tag that matches. The source describes bedding behaviour rather than naming a shelter resource.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights follow traits.diet. The water weight reflects the source's account of alligators grabbing deer 'as they try to drink from or cross bodies of water', which establishes deer as frequent water users. shrub_thicket at 0.8 is authored judgement from the bedding and fawn-hiding behaviour.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: 'White-tailed deer are generalists and can adapt to a wide variety of habitats' and 'They also eat hay, grass, white clover, and other foods they can find in a farmyard'; light_max is authored (judgement).

seasonal.strategy.note: Authored as ActiveYearRound: the source describes a resident generalist with a rut and a spring fawning season, and describes no migration or hibernation. PanTHERIA ActivityCycle 2 is not used for this field because the scale is undocumented in the file header.

seasonal.phases.note: Rut window from 'Females enter estrus ... normally in late October or early November, triggered mainly by the declining photoperiod', with the rut shorter in duration at higher latitude; fawning window from 'Females give birth to one to three spotted young ... in mid-to-late spring, generally in May or June', with weaning at 8-10 weeks. Exact window edges are judgements informed by those dates.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Juvenile duration from 'Fawns lose their spots during the first summer and weigh from 20 to 35 kg by the first winter' and the 8-10 week weaning (240 days used to reach the first-winter weight); 'Bucks are generally sexually mature at 1.5 years old' supports the adult stage at about that age. Scale is authored judgement and the fawn's 20-35 kg against a 65.7 kg adult is the basis for the 0.35 scale.

vocalizations.blow.note: 'White-tailed deer typically respond to the presence of potential predators by breathing very heavily (also called blowing) and fleeing. When they blow, the sound alerts other deer in the area', with the white tail flash adding to the warning.

vocalizations.grunt.note: From the Communication section: fawns give a high-pitched bleat that deepens into the mature deer's guttural grunt; does make maternal grunts when searching for bedded fawns; bucks grunt at a lower pitch still.

vocalizations.snort.note: 'In addition to grunting, both does and bucks also snort, a sound that often signals an imminent threat.' The same section adds that mature bucks produce a grunt-snort-wheeze pattern that asserts dominance, aggression and hostility.

vocalizations.note: All three descriptions are sourced from the Communication and predator-response sections; time windows and cooldowns are authored judgement, since no open source quantifies them. No frequency bands are given, so freq_hz is omitted.

look.note: Colours from the Description section: the coat is reddish-brown in spring and summer and turns grey-brown through fall and winter, and the species is characterised by 'the characteristic white underside to its tail'. The snout and tail are coloured from the markings slot and the legs from the accent slot; an enlarged tail part renders the white underside that gives the species its name, and a mirrored antler pair renders the buck's antlers. Proportions are authored judgement for a long-legged, deep-chested cervid with a raised neck.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared ground-forager program, which is written for a ground-dwelling mammal that forages, wanders, flees and rests in shelter. flee_m raised to 60 m and calm_m to 120 m for a large, wide-ranging deer; flee_gait set to gallop, matching the documented flight response and the predators' pursuit described in the source; forage_gait walk matches browsing. food_tag set to browse, the dominant diet share. rest_sun_lo_deg -18 and rest_sun_hi_deg 6 are authored for a crepuscular species, resting around the middle of the day and the middle of the night, which is a narrower band than the program's daytime default and follows the source's 'most active at dawn and dusk, sporadically resting throughout the day and night'.
